chapter.title: Scale From Zero to Millions of Users
chapter.source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
chapter.primary_goal: Understand how a simple application can evolve incrementally from a single-server system into an architecture capable of supporting millions of users.

chapter_summary.overview: The chapter demonstrates system scaling as an iterative architectural process. It starts with a single server containing the web application, database, cache, and other functionality. As traffic and data increase, responsibilities are separated into independently scalable tiers. The architecture progressively introduces dedicated databases, horizontal scaling, load balancing, database replication, caching, CDNs, stateless web servers, autoscaling, multiple data centers, message queues, observability and automation, and database sharding.
chapter_summary.central_principle: Do not begin with maximum complexity. Start with the simplest architecture that satisfies current requirements and introduce additional infrastructure as specific scalability, availability, performance, reliability, or operational problems emerge.
final_scaling_principles: Cache data as much as possible.
Host static assets in a CDN.
Scale the data tier through sharding when necessary.
Split tiers into individual services so they can scale independently.
Monitor the system and use automation tools.

learning_objectives.objective: Explain the complete request flow from DNS resolution to the web server response.
Explain why the web tier and data tier should eventually be separated.
Distinguish relational databases from non-relational databases and identify situations described in the chapter where NoSQL may be appropriate.
Compare vertical scaling with horizontal scaling and explain why horizontal scaling is preferred for large-scale applications.
Explain how load balancers improve scalability, availability, and failover of the web tier.
Explain database replication, read/write routing, replication benefits, and database failover.
Explain how caching reduces latency and database load and describe cache expiration, consistency, failure, overprovisioning, and eviction concerns.
Explain the CDN request flow and identify major considerations when using a CDN.
Distinguish stateful and stateless web architectures and explain why statelessness enables easier horizontal scaling and autoscaling.
Explain how geoDNS and multiple data centers improve availability and geographic performance.
Explain how message queues decouple producers and consumers and enable asynchronous processing.
Distinguish logging, metrics, monitoring, and automation concerns in a large-scale system.
Explain database sharding, sharding keys, hash-based routing, and major sharding challenges.

architecture_evolution.name: Single Server
architecture_evolution.new_problem: As the user base grows, one machine becomes insufficient and all components compete for the same server resources.

architecture_evolution.name: Separate Web Tier and Data Tier
architecture_evolution.change: Move the database onto a separate server from the web application.
architecture_evolution.benefit: The web tier and data tier can now be scaled independently.

architecture_evolution.name: Horizontal Web Scaling with Load Balancer
architecture_evolution.change: Add a load balancer and multiple web servers.
benefits: Incoming requests can be distributed among web servers.
A failed web server does not necessarily make the application unavailable.
Additional web servers can be added as traffic grows.

architecture_evolution.name: Database Replication
architecture_evolution.change: Introduce a master database and one or more slave databases.
architecture_evolution.write_path: Data-modifying operations are sent to the master database.
architecture_evolution.read_path: Read operations are normally sent to slave databases.
benefits: Improved read performance
Reliability
High availability

architecture_evolution.name: Cache Tier
architecture_evolution.change: Place frequently accessed or expensive-to-compute data in memory.
benefits: Lower response time
Reduced database workload
Cache infrastructure can scale independently

architecture_evolution.name: Content Delivery Network
architecture_evolution.change: Move static content such as images, JavaScript, CSS, and video closer to users.
benefits: Reduced static-content load on web servers
Improved load times for geographically distributed users

architecture_evolution.name: Stateless Web Tier
architecture_evolution.change: Move user session state out of individual web servers and into shared storage.
benefits: Requests can go to any web server.
Servers can be added and removed more easily.
Autoscaling becomes easier.
The web tier becomes more robust and scalable.

architecture_evolution.name: Multiple Data Centers
architecture_evolution.change: Deploy infrastructure across multiple geographic locations and use geoDNS for routing.
benefits: Users can be routed toward geographically closer infrastructure.
Traffic can be redirected to another data center during a major outage.

architecture_evolution.name: Message Queues and Independent Workers
architecture_evolution.change: Introduce asynchronous messaging between producers and consumers.
benefits: Decouples system components.
Producer and consumer can remain temporarily unavailable independently.
Workers can scale independently according to queue size.

architecture_evolution.name: Logging, Metrics, Monitoring, and Automation
architecture_evolution.change: Introduce operational tooling required to understand and manage a large system.
benefits: Detect system errors.
Understand system health.
Track business metrics.
Automate build, test, integration, and deployment processes.

architecture_evolution.name: Database Sharding
architecture_evolution.change: Partition database data across multiple database servers.
benefits: Scale storage horizontally.
Scale database traffic horizontally.

key_concepts.definition: The Domain Name System resolves a domain name into an IP address that the client can use to contact the system.
The network address returned after DNS resolution and used by a client to communicate with the server or load balancer.
The protocol used by clients to send requests to the web server in the chapter's architecture.
A commonly used API response format, especially for communication between mobile applications and web servers.
The application servers responsible for handling web or mobile traffic and application logic.
The database infrastructure responsible for storing and retrieving application data.
A database that represents data using tables and rows and supports SQL joins across tables.
A non-relational database category that includes key-value, graph, column, and document stores.
Increase the CPU, RAM, disk, or other resources of an existing machine.
Increase capacity by adding additional servers.
A component that distributes incoming traffic among a set of web servers.
An IP address reachable by servers within the same network but not directly reachable over the public internet.
Maintaining copies of database data on additional database servers.
Temporary in-memory storage for frequently accessed data or expensive responses so subsequent requests can be served faster.
The chapter's caching flow where the web server checks cache first, queries the database on a miss, stores the result in cache, and returns the result.
A policy determining when cached data should be removed or considered expired.
Removal of existing cache entries when the cache is full and space is required for new data.
Least Recently Used, described as the most popular cache eviction policy in the chapter.
Least Frequently Used, an alternative cache eviction policy.
First In First Out, another cache eviction policy.
Single Point of Failure: a component whose failure can stop the entire system from operating.
A geographically distributed network of servers used in this chapter primarily to cache and serve static content.
Time-to-Live, which specifies how long an object may remain cached before expiring.
The source from which a CDN obtains an asset when that asset is not currently cached at the CDN.
A server that remembers client state between requests.
A server that does not retain client state between requests; state is obtained from shared storage.
A load-balancing mechanism that repeatedly routes a client's requests to the same server.
Automatically adding or removing web servers based on traffic load.
A DNS service that resolves domain names to IP addresses based on the geographic location of the user.
A durable component used as a buffer for asynchronous communication between producers and consumers.
A service that creates messages and publishes them to a message queue.
A service that retrieves messages from a message queue and performs the associated work.
Horizontal database scaling that separates a large database into smaller independently stored partitions called shards.
One or more columns used to determine how data is distributed among shards.
Redistributing data and potentially changing the sharding function when existing shards no longer provide adequate capacity or distribution.
A condition where excessive requests are concentrated on one shard, potentially overloading it.
A workaround described for reducing the need for difficult joins across different database shards.

flashcards.front: What is the first step when a user accesses a domain such as api.mysite.com?
flashcards.back: DNS resolves the domain name and returns an IP address.

flashcards.front: What happens after the client receives the server's IP address?
flashcards.back: The client sends an HTTP request to the web server.

flashcards.front: What can the web server return to the client?
flashcards.back: HTML pages or a JSON response for rendering.

flashcards.front: Why separate the web tier from the database?
flashcards.back: Separating them allows the web tier and data tier to be scaled independently.

flashcards.front: What type of data structure characterizes relational databases?
flashcards.back: Tables and rows.

flashcards.front: What important operation is generally available in relational databases but generally unsupported by the NoSQL systems described in the chapter?
flashcards.back: Join operations across tables.

flashcards.front: What are the four NoSQL categories listed in Chapter 1?
flashcards.back: Key-value stores, graph stores, column stores, and document stores.

flashcards.front: When might the chapter suggest exploring a NoSQL database?
flashcards.back: When super-low latency is required, data is unstructured or non-relational, the application mainly serializes/deserializes data, or massive amounts of data must be stored.

flashcards.front: What is vertical scaling?
flashcards.back: Adding more CPU, RAM, disk, or other power to an existing server.

flashcards.front: What is horizontal scaling?
flashcards.back: Adding more servers to the resource pool.

flashcards.front: What are two major limitations of vertical scaling for the web tier?
flashcards.back: Hardware resources have a hard upper limit, and a single server lacks failover and redundancy.

flashcards.front: What is the primary role of a load balancer?
flashcards.back: To distribute incoming traffic among the web servers in a load-balanced set.

flashcards.front: Which public IP do users connect to after a load balancer is introduced?
flashcards.back: The public IP of the load balancer.

flashcards.front: How does the load balancer communicate with web servers in the chapter's architecture?
flashcards.back: Through their private IP addresses.

flashcards.front: What happens if one web server behind the load balancer goes offline?
flashcards.back: Traffic is routed to another healthy web server, and a replacement server can be added to the pool.

flashcards.front: Where are database writes sent in the chapter's replicated database architecture?
flashcards.back: To the master database.

flashcards.front: Where are database reads normally sent?
flashcards.back: To slave databases.

flashcards.front: Why are there often more slave databases than master databases?
flashcards.back: Most applications have substantially more reads than writes.

flashcards.front: What are the three replication advantages emphasized by the chapter?
flashcards.back: Better performance, reliability, and high availability.

flashcards.front: What can happen when the master database fails?
flashcards.back: A slave can be promoted to become the new master, although production promotion is more complicated if the slave is not fully up to date.

flashcards.front: What is the primary purpose of a cache?
flashcards.back: To store frequently accessed data or expensive responses in memory so later requests can be served faster.

flashcards.front: Describe the read-through cache flow in the chapter.
flashcards.back: Check cache first. On a cache hit, return the cached data. On a miss, query the database, store the returned data in cache, and return it to the client.

flashcards.front: What kind of data is particularly suitable for caching?
flashcards.back: Data that is read frequently and modified infrequently.

flashcards.front: Why should cache not be the only persistent storage for important data?
flashcards.back: Cache typically uses volatile memory, so its contents can be lost when the cache server restarts.

flashcards.front: What happens if cache expiration is too short?
flashcards.back: The application reloads data from the database too frequently.

flashcards.front: What happens if cache expiration is too long?
flashcards.back: Cached data can become stale.

flashcards.front: Why can cache consistency become difficult?
flashcards.back: Updates to the database and cache are not performed as one transaction, and multi-region deployments make synchronization even more challenging.

flashcards.front: What does overprovisioning cache memory accomplish?
flashcards.back: It provides additional capacity as memory usage grows.

flashcards.front: What is cache eviction?
flashcards.back: Removing existing cached items when the cache is full and space is needed for new entries.

flashcards.front: Which cache eviction algorithm does the chapter identify as the most popular?
flashcards.back: LRU, or Least Recently Used.

flashcards.front: What does a CDN primarily cache in this chapter?
flashcards.back: Static assets such as images, videos, CSS, and JavaScript.

flashcards.front: What happens on a CDN cache miss?
flashcards.back: The CDN requests the file from the origin, receives it, caches it according to its TTL, and returns it to the user.

flashcards.front: What is CDN TTL?
flashcards.back: The amount of time an asset remains cached before it expires.

flashcards.front: How can an asset be changed before its existing CDN TTL expires?
flashcards.back: Invalidate the object using the CDN provider's API or use object versioning, such as image.png?v=2.

flashcards.front: Why are stateful web servers difficult to scale?
flashcards.back: A user's requests may have to return to the specific server holding that user's state, making server addition, removal, and failure handling more difficult.

flashcards.front: Where is session state placed in a stateless web architecture?
flashcards.back: In shared storage outside the individual web servers.

flashcards.front: Why does statelessness make autoscaling easier?
flashcards.back: Because any request can be handled by any web server, servers can be added or removed without depending on locally stored client state.

flashcards.front: What does geoDNS do?
flashcards.back: It resolves domain names to IP addresses based on the geographic location of the user.

flashcards.front: What are three challenges of operating multiple data centers?
flashcards.back: Traffic redirection, data synchronization, and testing/deployment consistency.

flashcards.front: What is the fundamental purpose of a message queue?
flashcards.back: To provide a buffer for asynchronous communication between producers and consumers.

flashcards.front: Why does a message queue decouple producers and consumers?
flashcards.back: The producer can publish while the consumer is unavailable, and the consumer can process queued messages even when the producer is unavailable.

flashcards.front: How might worker count respond to message queue size?
flashcards.back: Add workers when the queue becomes large and reduce workers when the queue remains mostly empty.

flashcards.front: What three categories of metrics does Chapter 1 mention?
flashcards.back: Host-level metrics, aggregated-level metrics, and key business metrics.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of centralized logging?
flashcards.back: To aggregate error logs into a service where they can be searched and viewed more easily.

flashcards.front: What is sharding?
flashcards.back: Horizontal database scaling by separating a large database into smaller parts called shards.

flashcards.front: Do all shards necessarily have different schemas?
flashcards.back: No. The chapter's shards share the same schema while containing different data.

flashcards.front: What sharding function is used in the chapter's example?
flashcards.back: user_id % 4.

flashcards.front: What is arguably the most important decision in a sharding strategy according to the chapter?
flashcards.back: Choosing the sharding key so that data can be distributed evenly and queries can be routed efficiently.

flashcards.front: What is the celebrity problem in sharding?
flashcards.back: A hotspot-key problem in which a particular shard receives excessive traffic and becomes overloaded.

flashcards.front: Why can joins become difficult after sharding?
flashcards.back: The required records may reside on different database servers, making cross-shard joins difficult.

multiple_choice_questions.question: What is the correct high-level request sequence in the chapter's initial architecture?
choices: DNS lookup -> IP address -> HTTP request -> web server response
HTTP request -> DNS -> IP address -> web server
multiple_choice_questions.answer: DNS lookup -> IP address -> HTTP request -> web server response
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: The user first accesses a domain name, DNS returns an IP address, the client sends an HTTP request, and the web server returns HTML or JSON.

multiple_choice_questions.question: What is the primary benefit of separating the web server from the database server?
choices: The web tier and data tier can be scaled independently
multiple_choice_questions.answer: The web tier and data tier can be scaled independently
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Independent scaling is the major architectural reason given for separating the web and database tiers.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Which characteristic best matches a relational database as described in Chapter 1?
choices: Stores data in tables and rows and supports joins
Must always be distributed across many servers
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Stores data in tables and rows and supports joins
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: The chapter describes relational databases as table-and-row systems supporting SQL joins.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Which situation is specifically identified as a possible reason to consider a NoSQL database?
choices: The application has only one user
The application requires complex relational joins
multiple_choice_questions.answer: The application requires super-low latency
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Super-low latency is one of the explicit NoSQL use cases listed in the chapter.

multiple_choice_questions.question: What does scale up mean?
choices: Adding more resources to an existing server
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Adding more resources to an existing server
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Scale up is vertical scaling: increasing CPU, RAM, disk, or other resources on an existing machine.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Why does the chapter prefer horizontal scaling for large applications?
choices: Vertical scaling has hardware limits and poor redundancy characteristics
Vertical scaling can never increase performance
Horizontal scaling requires no additional infrastructure
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Vertical scaling has hardware limits and poor redundancy characteristics
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Vertical scaling eventually encounters hardware limits and does not inherently provide failover or redundancy.

multiple_choice_questions.question: After a load balancer is introduced, what should clients normally connect to?
choices: The public IP of the load balancer
The private IP of every web server
multiple_choice_questions.answer: The public IP of the load balancer
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Clients connect to the load balancer's public IP, and the load balancer communicates with web servers through private IPs.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Server 1 fails in a two-web-server load-balanced system. According to the chapter, what should happen?
choices: DNS should permanently remove the application
Traffic should be redirected to Server 2
All traffic should be sent directly to the database
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Traffic should be redirected to Server 2
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: The load balancer redirects traffic to the remaining healthy server, preventing the web tier from becoming unavailable.

multiple_choice_questions.question: In the replicated database model described in Chapter 1, which database normally handles writes?
multiple_choice_questions.answer: The master database
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Insert, update, delete, and other data-modifying commands are sent to the master database.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Why are multiple slave databases useful in a read-heavy system?
choices: Read queries can be processed in parallel across replicas
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Read queries can be processed in parallel across replicas
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Distributing read operations among slaves allows more queries to be processed in parallel.

multiple_choice_questions.question: What complication does the chapter identify when promoting a slave after master database failure?
choices: The slave may not have the most recent data
The slave contains only cached data
The load balancer cannot communicate with databases
multiple_choice_questions.answer: The slave may not have the most recent data
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: A slave might not be completely up to date, requiring recovery of missing data.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Which workload is best suited for caching according to the chapter?
choices: Data that cannot be lost and exists nowhere else
Data read frequently and modified infrequently
Data modified continuously and almost never read
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Data read frequently and modified infrequently
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Frequently read, infrequently modified information is a strong cache candidate.

multiple_choice_questions.question: A requested value is absent from cache. What happens next in the chapter's read-through flow?
choices: The web server queries the database, caches the returned result, and responds
The CDN is asked to perform the query
multiple_choice_questions.answer: The web server queries the database, caches the returned result, and responds
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: A cache miss causes the application to obtain the data from the database and populate the cache.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Why is an extremely short cache expiration period potentially harmful?
multiple_choice_questions.answer: It causes repeated database reloads
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Entries expire so quickly that the system repeatedly retrieves the same data from the database.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Why can an extremely long cache expiration period also be harmful?
choices: It forces every request to use the database
multiple_choice_questions.answer: It makes data stale
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Long-lived cache entries can continue serving information after the underlying data has changed.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Which cache eviction policy is identified as the most popular?
multiple_choice_questions.answer: LRU
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: The chapter identifies Least Recently Used as the most popular cache eviction policy.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Why would a system deploy multiple cache servers?
choices: To avoid a cache server becoming a single point of failure
multiple_choice_questions.answer: To avoid a cache server becoming a single point of failure
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: A single cache server can become a SPOF, so redundancy is recommended.

multiple_choice_questions.question: What content does the chapter primarily recommend placing in a CDN?
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Static assets
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Images, video, CSS, and JavaScript are the primary CDN content discussed.

multiple_choice_questions.question: A CDN receives a request for image.png but does not contain it. What should it do?
choices: Send the request to a slave database
Request the object from the origin
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Request the object from the origin
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: On a CDN miss, the CDN retrieves the asset from the origin.

multiple_choice_questions.question: What does a CDN TTL determine?
choices: How many web servers are available
Which sharding key should be selected
How long an object remains cached
multiple_choice_questions.answer: How long an object remains cached
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: TTL determines the lifetime of an object in the CDN cache.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Which is an appropriate CDN failure strategy according to the chapter?
choices: Allow clients to obtain the resource from the origin during a CDN outage
Route static resources into the database master
Make the CDN the only location containing the asset
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Allow clients to obtain the resource from the origin during a CDN outage
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: The chapter recommends considering fallback to the origin when the CDN becomes temporarily unavailable.

multiple_choice_questions.question: What is the central scaling problem with stateful web servers?
choices: Users may need to repeatedly reach the same server holding their state
The database can no longer store data
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Users may need to repeatedly reach the same server holding their state
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Local session state ties users to particular servers and complicates scaling and failure handling.

multiple_choice_questions.question: What architectural change makes the web tier stateless?
choices: Store additional state on every web server
Move all state into the CDN
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Move state into shared storage
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Removing session state from individual web servers allows any server to handle any request.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Why does statelessness work particularly well with autoscaling?
choices: New servers do not need preexisting local session state to handle requests
Each server owns a permanent set of users
It prevents servers from being removed
multiple_choice_questions.answer: New servers do not need preexisting local session state to handle requests
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Because state lives elsewhere, adding or removing application servers does not break a user's dependency on a specific machine.

multiple_choice_questions.question: What does geoDNS use when deciding which IP address to return?
multiple_choice_questions.answer: The user's geographic location
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: geoDNS can resolve a domain differently depending on where the user is located.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Which is NOT one of the three multi-data-center challenges emphasized by the chapter?
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Replacing HTTP with FTP
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Traffic routing, synchronization, and deployment consistency are the stated challenges.

multiple_choice_questions.question: What property of a message queue allows the producer and consumer to operate independently?
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Asynchronous buffering
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: The queue buffers messages, allowing production and consumption to occur asynchronously.

multiple_choice_questions.question: A photo-processing queue is growing rapidly. What scaling response does the chapter suggest?
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Add more workers
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Increasing the worker pool allows queued jobs to be processed faster.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Which of the following is a host-level metric listed in Chapter 1?
multiple_choice_questions.answer: CPU utilization
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: CPU, memory, and disk I/O are examples of host-level metrics.

multiple_choice_questions.question: What is database horizontal scaling called in the chapter?
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Sharding
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: The database-scaling section describes horizontal database scaling as sharding.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Using the chapter's example function user_id % 4, which shard stores user_id 14?
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Shard 2
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: 14 % 4 = 2, so the request is routed to shard 2.

multiple_choice_questions.question: What property is particularly important when selecting a sharding key?
choices: It should concentrate all users on one shard
It should help distribute data evenly
multiple_choice_questions.answer: It should help distribute data evenly
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Uneven distribution can cause shard exhaustion and hotspots, so even distribution is an important criterion.

multiple_choice_questions.question: Which situation may require resharding?
choices: A web server receives an HTTP request
A CDN has a cache hit
multiple_choice_questions.answer: A single shard reaches capacity
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Resharding may be required when a shard becomes full or uneven distribution causes some shards to become exhausted earlier than others.

multiple_choice_questions.question: A social network stores several extremely popular celebrity accounts on the same shard. What problem may occur?
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Hotspot key or celebrity problem
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Large amounts of traffic to the same shard can overload that shard.

multiple_choice_questions.question: What workaround does the chapter give for difficult joins across database shards?
multiple_choice_questions.answer: Denormalization
multiple_choice_questions.explanation: Denormalization can restructure data so needed queries can often be completed from a single table rather than requiring cross-shard joins.

true_false.statement: A relational database stores data using tables and rows.
true_false.explanation: This is the relational model described in Chapter 1.

true_false.statement: Horizontal scaling means increasing CPU and RAM on the same server.
true_false.explanation: That is vertical scaling. Horizontal scaling means adding servers.

true_false.statement: Clients normally communicate directly with individual private web-server IPs after the chapter introduces a load balancer.
true_false.explanation: Clients reach the public load-balancer IP; the load balancer communicates with the servers through private IPs.

true_false.statement: Database replication can improve performance, reliability, and availability.
In the chapter's replication model, all writes should normally go to slave databases.
true_false.explanation: Writes go to the master database.

true_false.statement: Cache is a safe replacement for persistent storage because its data always survives server restarts.
true_false.explanation: The chapter emphasizes that cache data is generally stored in volatile memory.

true_false.statement: Making cache expiration extremely short can increase database traffic.
LRU stands for Least Recently Used.
The chapter focuses primarily on using CDNs for static content.
A stateless server stores a user's session only on the local web server.
true_false.explanation: State is kept outside the web server in shared storage.

true_false.statement: Sticky sessions are one way to maintain user-to-server affinity in a stateful architecture.
geoDNS can route users based on their geographic location.
A producer must always wait until the consumer is available before publishing to a message queue.
true_false.explanation: The queue decouples them so a producer may publish even while the consumer is unavailable.

true_false.statement: All shards in the chapter's example have different schemas.
true_false.explanation: The shards share the same schema but contain different data.

true_false.statement: Sharding simplifies joins across multiple database servers.
true_false.explanation: Cross-shard joins become more difficult, which can lead to denormalization.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Vertical scaling increases the resources of an existing machine, such as CPU or RAM. Horizontal scaling adds additional machines. Vertical scaling is simple but ultimately limited by hardware capacity and does not inherently provide redundancy. Horizontal scaling is therefore more suitable for large-scale systems.

short_answer_questions.question: Why does a load balancer improve availability?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: A load balancer can route requests around an unavailable web server. With multiple web servers, failure of one server does not necessarily make the application unavailable because requests can be directed toward healthy servers.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain why database replication can improve read performance.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Writes are handled by the master while read operations can be distributed among multiple slave databases. This allows multiple read queries to execute in parallel and prevents one database from handling the full read workload.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain the tradeoff involved in choosing a cache expiration period.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: An expiration period that is too short creates unnecessary database reloads because entries expire frequently. An expiration period that is too long increases the chance of serving stale data.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is a stateless web tier preferable for horizontal scaling?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: When session state exists in shared storage rather than individual servers, any web server can process any user's request. Servers can therefore be added, removed, replaced, or autoscaled without maintaining user-to-server affinity.

short_answer_questions.question: What additional complications are introduced by multiple data centers?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The architecture must correctly redirect traffic, synchronize data between geographic locations, and ensure that testing and deployment keep services consistent across data centers.

short_answer_questions.question: How does a message queue improve system decoupling?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The producer places messages into a durable queue rather than depending directly on the consumer. The consumer processes queued work independently, so each side can temporarily be unavailable and can scale independently.

short_answer_questions.question: What kinds of metrics should a large system collect according to Chapter 1?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: The chapter describes host-level metrics such as CPU, memory, and disk I/O; aggregated metrics such as database-tier or cache-tier performance; and business metrics such as daily active users, retention, and revenue.

short_answer_questions.question: What makes a good sharding key?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: A good sharding key routes queries efficiently to the correct database and distributes data as evenly as possible so that individual shards do not become disproportionately full or overloaded.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is sharding not a free scalability solution?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Sharding introduces operational and data-model complexity. The chapter specifically identifies resharding, hotspot keys, and difficulty performing joins across shards.

common_confusions.confusion: Replication and sharding are the same thing.
common_confusions.correction: Replication copies data to additional databases. Sharding divides different portions of the dataset among different database servers.

common_confusions.confusion: A load balancer makes a web server more powerful.
common_confusions.correction: The load balancer distributes traffic across multiple servers; it enables horizontal scaling rather than increasing the hardware capacity of one server.

common_confusions.confusion: Cache and persistent storage are interchangeable.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter describes cache as temporary volatile storage. Important data should remain in persistent storage.

common_confusions.confusion: Stateless means the application has no user state.
common_confusions.correction: The application can still have user state. Stateless web servers simply keep that state outside the individual web servers in shared storage.

common_confusions.confusion: A CDN and application cache solve exactly the same problem.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter uses application caching primarily to reduce expensive or repeated data access and uses CDN caching primarily for geographically distributed static assets.

common_confusions.confusion: Sharding automatically solves every database scalability problem.
common_confusions.correction: Sharding introduces substantial complexity, including resharding, hotspots, and difficult cross-shard joins.

strong_answer_outline: Begin with a single server.
Separate the web tier and data tier.
Scale the web tier horizontally.
Add a load balancer.
Introduce database replication.
Add caching.
Move static assets to a CDN.
Make the web tier stateless.
Introduce autoscaling.
Support multiple data centers when geographic scale requires it.
Decouple expensive asynchronous tasks through message queues.
Introduce logging, metrics, monitoring, and automation.
Shard the database when vertical data-tier scaling is insufficient.

interview_style_questions.question: Your application is read-heavy. What techniques from Chapter 1 could reduce database pressure?
strong_answer_outline: Add read replicas so reads can be distributed.
Cache frequently accessed data.

Move appropriate non-relational workloads to a NoSQL data store when applicable.

interview_style_questions.question: What single points of failure exist as the architecture evolves, and how are they reduced?
strong_answer_outline: Single web server -> multiple servers plus load balancer
Single database -> database replication
Single cache server -> multiple cache servers
Single data center -> multiple data centers

strong_answer_outline: Scaling is iterative.
Vertical scaling can initially be simpler.
Sharding adds substantial complexity.

Use complexity when growth requirements justify it.

chapter_one_final_review.core_architecture_memory_chain: DNS -> Load Balancer -> Stateless Web Servers -> Cache/Data Tier/Message Queue -> Workers, with CDN for static content, database replication and later sharding for the data tier, plus multiple data centers, monitoring, logging, metrics, and automation.
chapter_one_final_review.one_sentence_takeaway: Scaling from zero to millions of users is a sequence of removing bottlenecks and single points of failure while making application and data components increasingly distributed, redundant, independently scalable, and observable.
